title: Estimate decimal sums and differences in real contexts (money, measurements)

lesson.title: Quick Guesses with Decimals: Estimate Like a Shopper

steps.say: You already know how to compare decimals and tell which one is bigger. Today we use that same skill for something super handy at the store: making a fast, smart guess about a total before you ever add the exact numbers.

Here is the trick. Slide each price to the nearest whole dollar on a number line. Three dollars and eighty-five cents sits between three and four, but look how close it snuggles up to four. So we say it is about four dollars.

visual.caption: 3.85 is much closer to 4 than to 3

steps.say: Now let us buy something at the school hot lunch. A hot chocolate costs three dollars and eighty-five cents, and a muffin costs two dollars and ten cents. Three eighty-five is about four. Two dollars and ten cents is just past two, so it is about two. Four plus two is six, so the total is about six dollars. When we add carefully we get five dollars and ninety-five cents, and look, that is just a nickel under our guess of six. Our estimate was great.

visual.caption: The real total, 5.95, lands right beside our estimate of 6

steps.say: Here is a mistake I see a lot. Some children just chop off the cents and say three eighty-five is three, and two ten is two, so the total is five dollars. But five is too low, because three eighty-five is almost four whole dollars. Chopping throws away eighty-five cents. Always ask which whole number is nearer on the number line, not which one comes first.

visual.caption: Chopping sends 3.85 back to 3, but it belongs near 4

steps.say: Estimating works for taking away, too. Your skipping rope is seven point eight metres long and your friend's is two point nine five metres. Seven point eight is about eight, and two point nine five is about three. On the number line, jumping from three up to eight is a jump of five. So the difference is about five metres. The exact answer is four point eight five metres, which is very close to five. Nice guess.

visual.caption: From about 3 to about 8 is a jump of about 5

steps.say: So remember, round each decimal to the nearest whole number first, then add or subtract those easy numbers. Your answer will not be exact, but it will be close enough to check if something makes sense.

lesson.answer: Round each decimal to the nearest whole number first, then add or subtract the easy numbers to get a close guess.

practice.question: At the farmers market you buy a basket of blueberries for six dollars and seventy-five cents and a loaf of bread for four dollars and twenty cents. Draw a number line from six to seven and mark six dollars and seventy-five cents. Which whole dollar is it closer to? Do the same for four dollars and twenty cents on a line from four to five. Then estimate the total.
practice.answer: Six dollars and seventy-five cents is closer to seven, and four dollars and twenty cents is closer to four. Seven plus four is eleven, so the total is about eleven dollars. The exact total is ten dollars and ninety-five cents, so the estimate is very close.
